## The folds that choose a model cannot also score it

[Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) chose a
tree's node size by cross-validation by site, and noted that the winner's error was a
little flattering, being the lowest of 12. With a hundred candidates, the winner can
carry columns of pure noise.
This page shows how to report a cross-validated score honestly when the same folds also
chose the model. That matters most when a survey is too small to set test sites aside,
which is common in marine work.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Out-of-fold predictions are pooled into one score

In cross-validation each station is predicted once, by the model fitted without its site.
That prediction is the station's **out-of-fold prediction**. Pooling the out-of-fold
predictions of every station and working out one RMSE from them gives the **pooled
score**.

[Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) averaged
the folds' own RMSEs instead. With five or ten folds of sites the two barely differ, but
the pooled score has one advantage: any scheme that holds out every station once scores
the same stations, so pooled scores from different schemes can be compared.
[Spatial and temporal cross-validation](spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) relies on this.

## Nested cross-validation scores the search as well

Choosing among candidates is part of building a model, whether the candidates are
settings, sets of inputs or methods. A search scores every candidate by cross-validation
and keeps the lowest. But each score is partly luck: these folds happen to suit some
candidates more than others. The lowest of many scores gathers the most luck, so the more
candidates there are, the more the winner's score flatters it. This is **selection
optimism**.

**Nested cross-validation** measures what the whole search is worth. An outer
cross-validation holds out one fold of sites at a time. Inside each outer round the search
runs in full on the remaining sites, with inner folds of its own, and chooses a candidate.
The chosen candidate is fitted to those sites and scored on the outer fold, which played
no part in the choice. The outer folds' predictions, pooled, score the search: how
well a model chosen this way predicts new sites.

::: {.diagram}
![Nested cross-validation. In each outer round, one fold of sites is held out and the search runs on the rest, scoring every candidate on inner folds of its own. The candidate it chooses is fitted to those sites and predicts the outer fold once. The outer folds' predictions, pooled into one score, score the search.](img/nested-cross-validation.svg){fig-alt="In outer round 1 of 5, the first of five folds of sites is held out and the other four are handed to the search. The search cuts those four folds into inner folds; in each inner round one inner fold is held out and every candidate is scored on it. The candidate with the lowest inner error is chosen, fitted to all four folds and used once to predict the outer fold. Three steps follow: repeat for each of the five outer folds; pool the outer folds' predictions into one score; that score is the search's, choice included. A note says the outer fold plays no part in the choice, so its error is not flattered by it."}
:::

A search therefore produces three things that are easy to confuse. The winner's
cross-validated score tells you which candidate to keep. The nested score is the one to
report. The final model, the winner refitted to all the data, has no score of its own: the
nested score is the best guess at how it will do on new sites.

## Worked example

The model is linear regression from
[Linear and polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd),
quick enough to fit thousands of times. Nested cross-validation needs no test sites, so this page uses
all the survey's sites. Every fold holds whole sites, as in
[Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd).

### Preparing the data

`fit_resamples()` fits a workflow in every round of the folds, and with `save_pred = TRUE`
it keeps the out-of-fold predictions; `collect_predictions()` gathers them, one per
station. In scikit-learn, `cross_val_predict()` does both.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
            "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude")

# linear regression on any set of inputs, with gaps filled inside each round
linear_on <- function(vars, data) {
  recipe(reformulate(vars, "abundance"), data = data) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    workflow(linear_reg())
}

cross_validate <- function(vars, data, folds) {
  fit_resamples(linear_on(vars, data), folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse),
                control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE))
}

# one RMSE from every station's out-of-fold prediction
pooled_rmse <- function(rounds) {
  collect_predictions(rounds) |> rmse(abundance, .pred) |> pull(.estimate)
}

tibble(stations = nrow(survey), sites = n_distinct(survey$site_id))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()
sites = survey["site_id"]

inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
          "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]

# linear regression on any set of inputs, with gaps filled inside each round
def linear_on(columns):
    numeric = [c for c in columns if c not in categorical]
    nominal = [c for c in columns if c in categorical]
    steps = [
        ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric),
        ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), nominal),
    ]
    # a candidate may have no numeric or no categorical inputs
    recipe = ColumnTransformer([step for step in steps if step[2]])
    return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", LinearRegression())])

# one RMSE from every station's out-of-fold prediction
def pooled_rmse(columns, data, folds, groups):
    predicted = cross_val_predict(linear_on(columns), data[columns],
                                  data["abundance"], cv=folds, groups=groups)
    return root_mean_squared_error(data["abundance"], predicted)

pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "sites": [sites.nunique()]})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: helpers
#| include: false
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
in_words <- function(n) {
  if (n > 10) return(as.character(n))
  c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")[n]
}
```

### A search over 100 sets of inputs picks noise

Twenty columns of random numbers, `noise_1` to `noise_20`, are added to the survey. They
carry no information about the catch. A search then draws 100 candidates, each linear
regression on five of the 28 columns, and scores every candidate by ten-fold
cross-validation by site.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: search
set.seed(21)
noise <- matrix(rnorm(nrow(survey) * 20), ncol = 20,
                dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("noise_", 1:20)))
noisy <- bind_cols(survey, as_tibble(noise))
columns <- c(inputs, colnames(noise))

candidates <- map(1:100, \(i) sample(columns, 5))
folds <- group_vfold_cv(noisy, group = site_id, v = 10)

searched <- map_dbl(candidates, \(vars) pooled_rmse(cross_validate(vars, noisy, folds)))
winner <- candidates[[which.min(searched)]]

tibble(best = min(searched), median = median(searched), worst = max(searched)) |>
  round(2)
winner
```

## Python

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.standard_normal((len(survey), 20)),
                     columns=[f"noise_{i}" for i in range(1, 21)])
noisy = pd.concat([survey, noise], axis=1)
columns = inputs + list(noise.columns)

candidates = [[str(c) for c in rng.choice(columns, 5, replace=False)]
              for i in range(100)]
folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=21)

searched = np.array([pooled_rmse(c, noisy, folds, sites) for c in candidates])
winner = candidates[searched.argmin()]

print(pd.DataFrame({"best": [searched.min()], "median": [np.median(searched)],
                    "worst": [searched.max()]}).round(2))
winner
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: search-numbers
#| include: false
winner_noise <- sum(str_starts(winner, "noise"))
winner_real <- setdiff(winner, colnames(noise))
real_sentence <- if (length(winner_real) > 0) {
  paste0("Its real ", if (length(winner_real) == 1) "input, " else "inputs, ",
         knitr::combine_words(winner_real, before = "`", oxford_comma = FALSE),
         ", carry what skill it has; the noise columns ride along because they happened ",
         "to suit these folds.")
} else ""
```

The winner scores `r f2(min(searched))`, the lowest of the 100, and
`r in_words(winner_noise)` of its five columns are noise.
`r real_sentence`
How much of its lead over the median candidate, `r f2(median(searched))`, is luck is
what the next part measures.

### Linear regression on the eight inputs beats the search's choice

The search is now run inside an outer five-fold cross-validation by site, with five inner
folds. For comparison, linear regression on the eight measured inputs, with no search, is
fitted and scored on the same outer folds.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: nested
set.seed(32)
outer <- group_vfold_cv(noisy, group = site_id, v = 5)

nested <- map(outer$splits, \(s) {
  fitting <- analysis(s)
  held <- assessment(s)
  inner <- group_vfold_cv(fitting, group = site_id, v = 5)
  inner_rmse <- map_dbl(candidates,
                        \(vars) pooled_rmse(cross_validate(vars, fitting, inner)))
  chosen <- candidates[[which.min(inner_rmse)]]
  predict_held <- function(vars) {
    predict(fit(linear_on(vars, fitting), fitting), held)$.pred
  }
  tibble(abundance = held$abundance,
         claimed = min(inner_rmse),
         searched = predict_held(chosen),
         eight_inputs = predict_held(inputs),
         noise_chosen = sum(str_starts(chosen, "noise")))
}) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "outer_fold")

nested |>
  summarise(`search claimed` = first(claimed),
            `search's choice, outer fold` = rmse_vec(abundance, searched),
            `eight inputs, outer fold` = rmse_vec(abundance, eight_inputs),
            `noise columns chosen` = first(noise_chosen),
            .by = outer_fold) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
outer = GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=32)

rounds = []
for k, (fit_rows, held_rows) in enumerate(outer.split(noisy, groups=sites), start=1):
    fitting, held = noisy.iloc[fit_rows], noisy.iloc[held_rows]
    inner = GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=k)
    inner_rmse = np.array([pooled_rmse(c, fitting, inner, fitting["site_id"])
                           for c in candidates])
    chosen = candidates[inner_rmse.argmin()]

    def predict_held(columns):
        fitted = linear_on(columns).fit(fitting[columns], fitting["abundance"])
        return fitted.predict(held[columns])

    rounds.append(pd.DataFrame({
        "outer_fold": k, "abundance": held["abundance"].to_numpy(),
        "claimed": inner_rmse.min(), "searched": predict_held(chosen),
        "eight_inputs": predict_held(inputs),
        "noise_chosen": sum(c.startswith("noise") for c in chosen)}))
nested = pd.concat(rounds, ignore_index=True)

(nested.groupby("outer_fold")
    .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({
        "search claimed": g["claimed"].iloc[0],
        "search's choice, outer fold": root_mean_squared_error(g["abundance"],
                                                               g["searched"]),
        "eight inputs, outer fold": root_mean_squared_error(g["abundance"],
                                                            g["eight_inputs"]),
        "noise columns chosen": g["noise_chosen"].iloc[0]}), include_groups=False)
    .reset_index()
    .round(2))
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: nested-numbers
#| include: false
per_fold <- nested |>
  summarise(claimed = first(claimed),
            searched = rmse_vec(abundance, searched),
            eight = rmse_vec(abundance, eight_inputs),
            noise = first(noise_chosen),
            .by = outer_fold)
claimed_mean <- mean(per_fold$claimed)
nested_searched <- rmse_vec(nested$abundance, nested$searched)
nested_eight <- rmse_vec(nested$abundance, nested$eight_inputs)
eight_wins <- sum(per_fold$eight < per_fold$searched)
noise_rounds <- if (n_distinct(per_fold$noise) == 1) {
  paste0("In every outer round, ", in_words(per_fold$noise[1]),
         " of the five columns it chose were noise.")
} else {
  paste0("In the five outer rounds it chose ",
         knitr::combine_words(per_fold$noise, oxford_comma = FALSE), " noise columns.")
}
wins_words <- if (eight_wins == 5) "all five" else paste(in_words(eight_wins), "of the five")
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-nested
#| fig-cap: "Each outer fold of the nested cross-validation: the error the search claimed for its choice on the inner folds, the error of that choice on the outer fold, and the error of linear regression on the eight measured inputs, with no search, on the same outer fold."
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("A dot plot with the five outer folds down the side and RMSE in individuals along the bottom. Each fold has three points. The search's claimed errors average {f2(claimed_mean)}. On the outer folds the search's choice lands to the right of its claim in {in_words(sum(per_fold$searched > per_fold$claimed))} of the five folds, and the model on the eight inputs lands to the left of the search's choice in {wins_words}.")
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
per_fold |>
  pivot_longer(c(claimed, searched, eight), names_to = "score", values_to = "rmse") |>
  mutate(score = factor(score, c("claimed", "searched", "eight"),
                        c("Search claimed", "Search's choice on the outer fold",
                          "Eight inputs, no search, on the outer fold")),
         outer_fold = factor(outer_fold, 5:1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(rmse, outer_fold)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = outer_fold), colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = score, shape = score), size = 3.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(ml_palette[c("grey", "vermilion", "blue")])) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16, 16)) +
  labs(x = "RMSE (individuals)", y = "Outer fold", colour = NULL, shape = NULL,
       title = paste("Eight inputs with no search beat the search's choice in",
                     wins_words, "folds")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::

The search claimed an average error of `r f2(claimed_mean)` on its inner folds. Pooled
over the outer folds, the models it chose score `r f2(nested_searched)`: that is the
nested score, and the honest figure for a model found by this search. On a single outer
fold the choice can do better than claimed, because some folds hold sites that are easier
to predict; pooled over all five, it does `r f2(nested_searched - claimed_mean)` worse.
That is a small gap: with `r nrow(survey)` stations and a model as simple as linear
regression, luck moves the scores little.

The search still did harm. `r noise_rounds` Linear regression on the eight
measured inputs, with no search at all, scores `r f2(nested_eight)` on the same outer
folds, and beats the search's choice in `r wins_words`. The search did not find a better
model; it found the candidates that suited its folds best.

Selection optimism grows with the number of candidates and with how flexible the models
are, and shrinks with the number of sites. A search over many settings of a flexible
model on a few dozen sites can flatter its winner badly, and only a nested score shows
by how much.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- Each station's **out-of-fold prediction** comes from the model fitted without its site,
  and the **pooled score** is one RMSE over all of them.
- The winner of a search has the lowest of many scores, and part of its lead is luck:
  **selection optimism**. It grows with more candidates, more flexible models and fewer
  sites. Here a search over 100 sets of inputs kept random columns.
- **Nested cross-validation** runs the whole search inside each outer round and scores
  its choice on the outer fold. It put the search at `r f2(nested_searched)`, a little
  worse than claimed and behind the eight measured inputs with no search
  (`r f2(nested_eight)`). Report the nested score, not the winner's.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Add the eight measured inputs to the candidates as a 101st set. Does the search choose
   it, and how far does the nested score move?
2. Draw 1,000 candidates instead of 100. Does the winner's claimed score fall, and does
   the nested score follow it?
3. Run the search and the nested cross-validation on 40 sites drawn at random. Predict
   first: does the gap between the claimed and the nested score grow?
